opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. When I started working on reinforcement learning, a lot of the excitement came from settings like Atari games or board games. Those are clean environments. You have a well-defined state, a fixed set of actions, a clear reward signal, and you can run millions of episodes in simulation. That's a great sandbox for developing algorithms, but it's quite far from how most real-world problems look.

What struck me as missing was really a few things.

The first is **prior knowledge**. Classical RL agents essentially start from scratch, a blank slate. They have to learn everything, including basic facts about the world, purely through trial and error. Humans don't operate that way. If you hand someone a new video game or a new piece of software, they bring an enormous amount of background knowledge about how things generally work. Without that, RL is incredibly sample-inefficient, and in practical applications you just can't afford millions of interactions, especially when each interaction is expensive or involves a real person.

The second is **language**. So much of how we communicate goals, describe environments, and transfer knowledge happens through language. Instruction manuals, documentation, someone telling you "don't touch that, it's hot." Classical RL had no natural way to use any of that. A big part of my early work was asking: can an agent read text, whether it's a description of the game or the rules, and use that to learn faster or generalize to new environments? That turned out to help quite a bit.

The third is **specifying the task itself**. In classical RL, someone has to carefully engineer a reward function. In the real world, goals are fuzzy, they're often expressed in natural language, and getting the reward wrong leads to all kinds of strange behavior. So there's a gap between "what the user actually wants" and "the scalar number the algorithm optimizes."

And finally, **generalization**. Agents trained on one environment tended to be brittle. Change the layout or the setting a little and performance would collapse.

So in many ways the question I kept coming back to was: how do we give these agents a richer understanding of the world, and language seemed like the natural bridge. That line of thinking is actually part of what led into the work on pretraining language models. If you can learn general-purpose knowledge from large amounts of text first, you have a much better starting point for any downstream task, including decision-making. In hindsight, that combination of pretrained language knowledge with RL-style interaction is pretty much what we see in today's language agents.

r001.rationale: The response discusses sample inefficiency and other practical gaps, but does not state that theoretical convergence to an optimal policy is insufficient.

r002.rationale: The response says real-world interactions can be expensive, but does not mention repeatedly destroying a robot or that this cost is unacceptable.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So when I was doing my PhD at MIT, I was working on reinforcement learning, and specifically on applying it to language problems, text-based games and things like that. And what struck me very quickly was that classical RL, the way it was formulated, assumed you had this very clean setup: a fixed set of states, a fixed set of actions, a reward signal that comes back reliably, and crucially, that you could interact with the environment as many times as you wanted. Millions of episodes if necessary.

And none of those assumptions really hold in the real world. If you think about a robot, or a dialogue system, or anything that has to operate with people, you can't afford millions of trials. The action space isn't a small discrete set, it's often enormous or essentially open-ended, like language. And the rewards are sparse, delayed, and sometimes ambiguous.

But the thing I felt was most missing was prior knowledge. Classical RL agents start from zero every time. They have no idea what a door is, or what "pick up the key" means, or that fire is dangerous. A human playing a new game for the first time brings an enormous amount of knowledge about how the world works, and that's what lets them learn in a handful of tries instead of a million. So a lot of my work was asking: how do you get that kind of knowledge into an agent? And language turned out to be a really natural vehicle for that, because language is this compressed encoding of what humans know about the world. If an agent can read, it can bootstrap.

The other piece was generalization. Classical RL was very good at mastering one environment and then completely failing on a slightly different one. Change the layout of the maze, change the colors, and the policy falls apart. For anything practical you need agents that transfer, that carry over what they've learned. And that's really a representation learning problem as much as it's an RL problem, which is part of what eventually pulled me toward the pretraining work. The idea that you could learn general-purpose representations from large amounts of unlabeled data and then adapt them to a task with very little supervision, that was addressing exactly the gap I'd been bumping up against in RL.

r001.rationale: The response discusses practical limits of classical RL, but does not mention theoretical convergence to an optimal policy or say that convergence alone is insufficient.

r002.rationale: It says robots cannot afford millions of trials, but does not identify repeatedly destroying a robot during training as an unacceptable cost.

astra-6.text:
One thing I felt was missing was the ability to use knowledge that’s already available in language. In the classical reinforcement learning setup, an agent learns by interacting with an environment and getting rewards. But it often starts from scratch, which can require a huge amount of trial and error.

Humans don’t learn that way exclusively. We can read instructions, ask someone for advice, or draw on something we learned in a different setting. If you’re learning a new game, you can read the rules before you start playing. I was interested in how we could give reinforcement learning agents that same ability—using language to guide exploration and transfer knowledge, rather than having to discover everything through experience.

r001.rationale: The response discusses learning from language and trial and error, but does not state that theoretical convergence to an optimal policy is insufficient for practical use.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention robots being repeatedly destroyed or the cost of that during physical training.

sol-6.1.text:
One thing I felt was missing was the ability to use knowledge that doesn’t come directly from interacting with an environment. In the classical reinforcement learning setup, an agent takes actions, gets rewards, and learns through trial and error. But if you’re starting from scratch every time, that can require a huge amount of experience, which is difficult in practical settings.

Humans don’t learn that way exclusively. We can read instructions, get advice, or bring what we learned in one situation to another. Language seemed like a natural way to give agents access to that kind of knowledge. So the question for me was: how can we combine learning from interaction with learning from what people have already written or told us?

r001.rationale: The candidate says trial-and-error learning may require a huge amount of experience, but does not mention theoretical convergence to an optimal policy or explain that convergence alone fails to make RL practical.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not mention robots, physical training, or the cost of repeatedly destroying a robot.
